PREFACE 


It  must  have  been  between  1882  and  1885  that  Mr.  Henry 
Bradshaw  pointed  out  to  me  the  need  of  a  new  edition  of  the  Sarum 
Missal  based  upon  the  manuscripts.  Excellent  as  the  Burntisland 
edition  is,  yet  its  text  was  drawn  mainly  from  the  printed  books, 
and  thus  fails  to  give  precise  knowledge  of  the  rite  as  it  was 
before  printing  came  into  existence  in  the  latter  half  of  the  fifteenth 
century.  A  rite  known  as  the  Sarum  was  well  recognized  in  the 
thirteenth  century.  There  is  the  tradition  that  St.  Osmund,  who 
died  in  1099,  had,  with  the  consent  of  the  Chapter,  settled  cer- 
tain rules  for  the  worship  of  the  divine  name  ;  and  it  was  claimed 
for  the  customs  of  Salisbury  in  1256  that  they  were  as  the  sun  in 
the  heavens  whose  rays  shed  light  upon  other  churches,^  a  claim 
which  is  sustained  by  the  inquiry  *  what  the  Sarum  customs  were ' 
made  three  years  later  by  the  church  of  Glasgow  of  the  Dean 
and  Chapter  of  Salisbury .^  Still  earlier  in  the  thirteenth  century 
the  expression  secundum  consuctudineni  or  ordinale  Sarum  appears. 
In  1223  the  Bishop  and  Chapter  of  St.  Davids  determined  that 
certain  services  should  be  secundum  Ordinale  Ecclesiae  Sarum? 
The  Bishop  of  Winchester  in  1226  ordered  that  in  the  College  of 
Merewell  the  divine  service  should  be  secundum  Sareshiriam.^ 
And  in  1228  Gregory  IX  affirms  that  the  institutions  of  St.  Osmund 
have  been  followed  by  the  greater  part  of  England.^  Thence- 
forward the  expression  secundum  tistim  Sarum  becomes  well 
established.

1737,  vol.  i.  p.  715. 

*  Wilkins,  idid.  p.  741. 

'  A.  W.  Haddan  and  W.  Stubbs,  Councils  ana  Ecclesiastical  Documents,  Clarendon 
Press,  1869,  vol.  i.  p.  459.

PREFACE 


It  was  a  recension  of  this  early  form  of  the  Sarum  Missal,  as  it 
existed  soon  after  the  time  of  St.  Osmund,  that  was  to  be  sought 
for.  But,  unhappily,  even  with  the  aid  of  the  Rev.  Dr.  Bannister, 
who  is  at  home  in  all  the  libraries  of  Europe,  no  manuscript  of  the 
twelfth  century  could  be  found.  At  last  a  manuscript,  at  that 
time  belonging  to  the  late  Earl  of  Crawford  and  Balcarres,  was 
found,  which  in  the  opinion  of  Sir  Edward  Maunde  Thompson  was 
written  in  the  thirteenth  century,  and  his  opinion  was  endorsed  by 
the  presence  in  the  manuscript  of  the  following  note  :  Memoriale 
Henrici  de  Cicestria  Canonici  Exon.  precij  Ix.  s.  Commenting  on  this 
Sir  Edward  Maunde  Thompson  observes  that  '  Henry  of  Chichester 
was  precentor  of  Crediton  and  resigned  his  office  in  1364.  We 
have  thus  an  approximate  date  for  the  volume,'  ^  In  the  book 
there  was  also  at  the  end  of  the  Order  of  the  Mass  the  statement : 
Sicque  completur  officiunt  misse  secundum,  usum  Sariim^  which 
seems  by  itself,  even  if  we  put  aside  indications  in  other  parts  of 
the  book,  some  proof  of  its  relations  to  Salisbury.  Thus  we  have 
evidence  both  of  the  century  in  which  the  book  was  written  and  of 
the  church  whose  use  it  presents. 

But  there  is  further  evidence  both  of  age  and  church.  In  the 
Calendar  of  this  Mass-Book  there  is  on  September  15  the  entry 
Festivitas  religuiarum  Sarum.  This  is  again  evidence  that  we  are 
dealing  with  a  Salisbury  book.  And  as  to  age  it  would  be  some 
evidence  that  the  book  was  written  before  1319  and  after  1150: 
for  in  1 150,  or  thereabouts,  the  feast  of  relics  was  fixed  on 
September  15  by  Bishop  Jocelyn^  ;  and  in  1319  the  day  of  this 
feast  was  changed  from  September  15  to  the  Sunday  after  the 
Translation  of  St.  Thomas  of  Canterbury  in  July.^  So  that  the 
time  of  writing  the  book  may  be  inferred  to  be  some  year  between 
1150  and  1319. 

The  fact  that  the  manuscript  contains  no  mention  of  the  feast  of 
Corpus  Christ!  is  also  in  favour  of  an  early  date.  The  first  beginnings 
of  this  festival  are  thought  to  have  arisen  in  1246  at  Liege,  a  place

If  we  allow  these  premisses,  it  seems  not  impossible  that  the

By  the  aid  of  the  Rev.  Dr.  Bannister,  I  was  enabled  in  1904  to 
bring  out  a  list  of  some  fifty-eight  Sarum  manuscript  missals  from 
different  parts  of  Europe,  and  the  list  appears  in  my  volume  of 
Tracts  on  the  Mass^  By  the  same  kind  assistance  I  am  now  able 
to  add  some  few  more. 

The  Morris  Missal,  before  1332,  now  in  the  Pierpont  Morgan

Recently,  I  have  heard  through  the  Rev.  Dr.  J.  T.  Fowler,  Hon. 
Canon  of  Durham,  of  two  other  manuscript  Sarum  Missals,  and 
possibly  a  third,  in  the  possession  of  Mr.  J.  Meade  Falkner,  of 
Durham.  One  of  these  appears  to  have  been  written  for  Closworth, 
Dorset,  and  another  for  Buckland.  The  Buckland  MS.  is  thought 
to  have  been  written  about  1380  ;  the  Closworth  about  1400. 

Comparing  all  the  known  Sarum  manuscript  missals  together, 
it  appeared  that,  next  to  the  Crawford  Missal,  the  earliest  were  two 
manuscripts  :  one,  in  the  Library  of  the  Arsenal  at  Paris  ;  and  the 
other,  in  the  Library  of  the  University  of  Bologna.  In  importance 
they  seemed  to  be  second  only  to  the  missal  belonging  to  Lord 
Crawford.

The  former  of  these  two  is  the  missal  at  the  Library  of  the 
Arsenal  in  Paris,  No.  135,  of  which  the  symbol  in  this  work  is  A. 
My  attention  was  first  directed  to  it  as  being  of  Canterbury  Use; 
but  on  examination  it  proved  to  be  of  Sarum  Use.^  As  in  the 
Crawford  Missal,  the  feast  of  relics  is  kept  on  September  15  and 
there  is  no  celebration  of  Corpus  Christi.  Judging  from  the  roto- 
graphs  Sir  George  Warner  thought  the  writing  to  be  of  the  latter 
half  of  the  thirteenth  century,  towards  its  end ;  Mr.  Falconer 
Madan  places  it  about  1300. 

I  may  gratefully  make  mention  of  the  fact  that  I  owe  the 
possession  of  the  rotographs  of  this  manuscript  to  the  kind  inter- 
vention of  Monsieur  Henri  Omont,  who  asked  that  the  manuscript 
of  the  Arsenal  should  be  sent  to  the  National  Library,  where  I  was 
thus  able  to  have  the  book  rotographed  under  his  supervision. 

From  the  numerous  notes  added  to  the  manuscript  it  may  be 
safely  inferred  that  it  was  carried  from  England  into  France,  and, 
from  the  allusions  to  the  customs  of  the  Pictavienses,  to  the 
neighbourhood  of  Poitiers.  These  notes,  being  French,  have  not 
usually  been  introduced  into  the  collation. 

The  second  manuscript  collated  is  a  Sarum  missal  in  the  Library 
of  the  University  of  Bologna,  No.  2565,  for  the  knowledge  of  which 
I  am  indebted  to  the  Rev.  Dr.  Bannister.  There  is  no  feast  of 
relics  marked  in  the  Calendar  on  September  15.  Octava  S.  Marie 
takes  that  place ;  while  after  the  day  of  the  translation  of  St.  Thomas 
of  Canterbury  in  July  there  has  been  added  to  the  Calendar^  in 
a  later  hand  a  note  that  the  feast  of  relics  is  to  be  kept  in  the 
church  of  Salisbury  on  the  Sunday  after  the  translation  of 
St.  Thomas  ;  but  that  in  this  missal  the  feast  of  relics  with  its 
service  will  be  found  in  the  octaves  of  the  Nativity  of  Blessed 
Mary.  So  indeed  it  is ;  also  accompanied  by  a  marginal  note 
repeating  in  substance  what  has  been  said  in  the  Calendar.^  The 
symbol  of  this  manuscript  in  this  present  edition  is  B. 

From  the  presence  of  a  mass  of  St.  Frideswide  in  the  Sanctoralc^ 
it  has  been  thought  that  the  missal  was  written  for  Oxford.     The

Clerks  of  the  Oxford  Colleges,  even  though  Oxford  were  in  the 
diocese  of  Lincoln,  were  bound  by  oath  to  follow  the  use  of  Sarum.^ 
The  Calendar  has  many  additions,  noting  the  obits  of  the  Mowbray 
family,  and  of  persons  connected  with  it. 

Sir  George  Warner,  again  judging  from  the  rotographs,  thinks 
that  the  handwriting  of  B  is  early,  quite  early,  in  the  fourteenth 
century.  With  this  Mr.  Falconer  Madan  agrees,  ascribing  the  hand 
to  the  first  quarter  of  the  fourteenth  century. 

It  must  be  regretted  that  the  manuscript  is  imperfect  through  the 
withdrawal  by  some  profane  hand  of  many  leaves  and  many 
initials.  These  losses  have  been  indicated  in  the  notes  to  the  text 
below.  There  remain  now  some  625  pages,  the  manuscript  having 
been  numbered  by  pages  and  not  by  leaves. 

For  obtaining  permission  from  the  authorities  at  Rome  for  the 
rotographing  of  this  manuscript  I  am  indebted  to  the  Rev.  Dr. 
Bannister,  who  exerted  his  influence  with  the  Italian  officials  to 
lighten  the  burden  that  would  otherwise  have  been  incurred. 

Thus  it  seemed  well  to  take  for  the  text  of  the  following  edition 
the  manuscript  that  then  belonged  to  Lord  Crawford.  It  was 
Sarum ;  and  the  earliest  missal  of  that  rite  known  to  us.  Also  it 
was  complete.  It  had  not  lost  the  large  number  of  leaves  that 
have  been  torn  out  of  the  missal  from  Bologna ;  and  it  had  not  the 
large  number  of  textual  errors  which  appear  in  the  missal  from 
the  Library  of  the  Arsenal  at  Paris,  and  which  indicate  a  some- 
what careless  scribe.  But  the  early  date  of  these  two  Sarum 
Missals  pointed  them  out  as  useful  for  collation  with  the  probably 
older  text  of  Lord  Crawford's  book,  more  carefully  written,  and 
complete. 

During  the  work  of  collation,  occasional  notes  have  been  added 
from  other  manuscripts  of  the  Sarum  Rite,  especially  from  a  missal 
formerly  in  the  possession  of  the  late  Mr.  William  Morris,  who  in  his 
lifetime  gave  me  leave  to  take  notes  of  the  work  and  to  photograph 
the  illuminations.  This  was  also  an  early  missal.  Sir  George 
Warner  was  inclined  to  think  that  it  was  written  about  1320,  and 
Lord  Dillon,  from  the  armour  shown  on  some  of  the  illuminations, 
that  they  were  produced  about  1320.     The  feast  of  relics  is  still  in

Society,  1894.    Defensorium  Directorii,  p.  6,  §  [3].

the  Calendar  on  September  15.  The  Ordinary  of  the  Mass  of  this 
manuscript  has  been  edited  ^  up  to  the  point  where  unfortunately  it 
becomes  imperfect,  that  is,  in  the  middle  of  the  prayer  Domine

In  a  large  number  of  masses  only  the  incipit  to  the  processional 
anthem  has  been  given  in  the  Crawford  Missal.  Where  this  is  the 
case  it  has  been  thought  well  to  supply,  for  the  convenience  of 
the  student,  in  a  note  in  the  lower  margin,  the  words  wanting  in  the 
Crawford  Missal.  These  have  been  taken  from  a  Bodleian  MS. 
Liturg.  408,  formerly  MS.  Add.  B.  20,  a  Sarum  Processional  of 
the  latter  half  of  the  fourteenth  century,  if  we  follow  the  catalogue. 
The  symbol  used  for  this  manuscript  is  P. 

As  early  as  1899  the  late  Lord  Crawford  was  approached  with 
a  request  to  allow  his  magnificent  manuscript  to  be  transcribed. 
With  his  invariable  courtesy  and  generosity  he  allowed  the  precious 
missal  to  be  deposited  in  the  Library  of  the  University  of  Aberdeen, 
where  Mr.  F.  C.  Eeles  had  most  obligingly  offered  to  undertake 
the  work  of  transcription.  Much  assistance  in  making  these 
arrangements  was  given  by  the  late  Mr.  Edmond,  then  Librarian 
at  Haigh  Hall,  and  by  Mr.  P.  J.  Anderson,  the  Librarian  at 
Aberdeen.  Transcription  by  Mr.  Eeles  was  continued  until  more 
than  two-thirds  of  the  manuscript  had  been  copied  out,  and  the 
leaves  of  his  excellent  transcript  were  ready  to  be  sent  to  the 
printers,  when  the  book  was  suddenly  recalled  in  August,  1901, 
owing  to  a  change  in  ownership. 

All  further  work  upon  the  manuscript  ceased  until  close  upon 
1909.  The  manuscript  had  meantime  been  left  to  the  John 
Rylands  Library  at  Manchester  ;  and  permission,  for  which  I  would 
express  my  sincere  thanks,  was  given  by  the  Trustees,  to  have  the 
book  rotographed.  This  being  done,  what  remained  to  be  tran- 
scribed was  copied  from  the  rotograph  by  Miss  E.  Margaret 
Thompson.  When  the  whole  of  the  text  had  thus  been  prepared, 
it  was  compared  with  the  rotograph  of  the  Crawford  Missal  which 
was  read  to  me  by  my  son.     I  must  also  speak  of  my  great  debt

XI 


to  Mr.  T.  Gambier-Parry,  who  read  to  me,  for  purposes  of  com- 
parison, the  whole  of  the  rotographs  of  the  Sarum  Missals  from 
the  Arsenal  and  from  Bologna,  which  have  already  been  spoken  of. 
After  the  copy  had  been  set  up,  the  proofs  were  read  by  Miss 
E.  G.  Parker  with  the  three  sets  of  rotographs. 

The  scheme  of  transcription  was  as  follows.  The  contractions  of 
the  manuscripts  were  expanded  in  accordance  with  well-known 
palaeographical  rules.  The  spelling  of  the  Crawford  Missal  was 
closely  followed ;  but  the  variations  in  spelling  of  the  other  two 
manuscripts  neglected.  Then,  as  a  rule,  when  the  order  of  the 
words  in  A  and  B  varied  from  that  in  C,  no  notice  was  taken  of 
the  difference.  The  scribal  errors  are  numerous  in  A,  and  the 
change  of  position  of  the  words  appears  to  be  often  the  result  of 
•caprice.  For  example,  qiiaesimms  Domine  may  appear  in  A  as 
Domine  quaesmmis,  but  variants  of  this  nature  in  either  A  or  B 
have  not  been  reproduced. 

Secretum  has  been  found  in  most  cases  in  C  where  the  title  of 
the  secret  prayer  at  the  offertory  has  been  written  in  full ;  and  in 
this  form  it  has  been  thought  well  to  print  it  in  the  following  pages. 
SecreUcm  is  by  no  means  uncommon  in  later  Sarum  missals. 

In  place  of  Offertorium  A  has  often  Offercnda  if  there  be  room ; 
and  in  place  of  Oracio  it  has  frequently  Collecta.  Where  C  has 
Amen,  A  will  often  have  Euotiae  (the  vowels  of  seculorum  Amen), 
but  these  variants  have  not  always  been  noticed.  Secreta,  not 
Secretum,  is  the  expanded  form  in  A  of  the  title  for  the  secret 
prayer  after  the  offertory. 

Clarendon  type  has  been  used  for  the  titles  of  the  masses  and 
•other  services  in  order  to  make  these  descriptions  more  apparent  to 
the  reader.  In  accordance  with  usual  custom  the  additions  of  the 
editor  are  enclosed  in  square  brackets. 

When  it  is  wished  to  call  attention  to  the  spelling  of  a  word  as 
being  the  exact  following  of  the  spelling  of  the  manuscript,  an 
obelus  has  been  set  immediately  after  the  word. 

After  consultation  with  the  Rev.  G.  H.  Palmer  it  was  determined 
not  to  reproduce  the  music  which  is  attached  to  the  offices,  grails, 
offertories,  and  communions  or  any  other  part  of  the  book.  A  good 
edition  of  the  Gradual  had  recently  appeared,^  and  the  music  in  the 

^  Graduale  Sarisburiense,  Plain  song  and  Mediaeval  Music  Society,  ed.  W.  H.  Frere, 
London, 1894. 


xii  PREFACE 

manuscript  varied  so  little  from  that  in  the  edition  that  it  was  not 
advisable  to  produce  again  the  same  music  at  so  short  an  interval 
of  time. 

Following  the  variations  in  the  size  of  the  written  letters  in 
the  Crawford  manuscript,  the  size  of  the  type  in  this  edition  has 
also  been  varied.  The  liturgical  sections  accompanied  by  musical 
notes,  such  as  the  offices,  grails,  offertories,  and  communions,  and  in 
general  all  parts  that  are  to  be  sung,  are  in  a  much  smaller  hand 
than  the  collects  and  lessons  of  the  Mass.  Accordingly  these  latter 
are  printed  in  larger  type  while  the  former  are  in  smaller.^  Other 
parts  such  as  the  Canon  of  the  Mass  and  the  Preccs  in  Prostratione 
are  in  larger  writing  still,  and  thus  are  printed  below  in  larger 
type  again.^ 

Accompanying  the  Catalogue  of  the  Manuscripts  in  the  John 
Rylands  Library  at  Manchester  which  Dr.  Montague  James,  the 
Provost  of  King's  College,  Cambridge,  is  now  editing,  there  will 
be,  he  is  so  good  as  to  tell  me,  six  photographic  reproductions  of 
pages  in  the  Crawford  Missal.  One  of  these  will  be  the  page 
which  gives  the  Advent  introit,  Ad  te  levavi  animmn  meant,  on 
fo.  1 6,  and  another  the  page  containing  the  beginning  of  the  Canon 
of  the  Mass.^ 

The  lessons  of  the  Mass  have  not,  as  a  rule,  been  given  in  full. 
In  general  they  agreed  so  closely  with  the  corresponding  passages 
in  Vercellone's  edition  of  the  Vulgate  which  was  issued  at  Paris 
in  1891,  that  it  was  considered  unnecessary  to  reproduce  more  than 
the  beginning  and  the  ending  of  the  lessons.  In  some  cases  where 
the  text  varied  considerably  from  that  of  the  Vulgate  the  text  of  the 
lesson  has  been  given  in  full.  For  example,  the  prophetical  lesson 
for  the  Octave  of  the  Epiphany  ^  is  not  from  the  Vulgate  ;  and 
the  Rev.  H.  J.  White  writes :  '  It  is  an  interesting  relic  of  Old- 
Latin  translation  which  has  survived,  in  the  strange  way  in  which 
older  versions  do  last  on,  in  liturgical  books ;  it  is  of  course  trans- 
lated from  the  LXX,  not  from  the  Hebrew.'  References  to  the 
Vulgate  are  given  together  with  the  titles  of  the  lessons.  Where 
the  page  of  the  manuscript  ends  in  some  part  of  the  lesson,  the 
words  at  which  the  turn  is  made  are  given  in  the  middle  of  the 

^  See  below,  for  examples  of  this,  p.  21.  "^  See  below,  pp.  209  and  32 1. 

*  See  below,  pp.  14  and  221.  *  See  below,  p.  39. 


PREFACE  xiii 

runners.     The  indication  of  the  page  is  given   at  the  end  of  the 
line.^ 

It  should  be  noticed  that  the  book  is  a  complete  missal ;  indeed 
it  contains  more  than  is  commonly  found  in  later  missals.  For 
instance,  the  processional  is  usually  a  book  by  itself;  but  here  the 
anthems  for  the  procession  may  often  be  found  at  the  beginning  of 
each  mass  for  the  Sunday  or  certain  other  holidays.  There  are 
also  several  offices  from  the  Manual,  such  as  baptism,^  marriage,^ 
visitation  of  the  sick,^  and  burial  of  the  dead.^  There  are  even 
fragments  from  the  Pontifical,  the  form  for  confirmation,^  and  for 
reconciling  penitents  on  Maundy  Thursday.^  Adest  o  venerabilis 
pontifex  ^  comes  by  itself  after  the  Ordinary  of  the  Mass. 

In  this  volume,  it  appears  to  me,  it  would  be  out  of  place  to 
attempt  to  discuss  fully  the  relation  of  the  Sarum  rite  to  other 
Western  Uses,  or  to  trace  in  detail  the  variations  which  may  be 
observed  in  manuscripts  and  printed  texts  of  the  Sarum  liturgy 
between  the  period  of  the  manuscripts  employed  for  this  edition  and 
the  time  at  which  the  rite  was  laid  aside.  Any  adequate  treatment 
of  either  of  these  matters  would  require  an  extension  of  the  bulk  of 
the  book  beyond  reasonable  limits :  and  both  of  them  will,  I  hope, 
be  rendered  more  easy  of  investigation  by  the  providing  of  an 
edition  of  the  earliest  accessible  text  of  the  Missal.  It  is  in  this 
hope  that  I  have  carried  out  the  work  of  editing  the  present 
volume. 

But  without  entering  far  into  these  matters,  I  think  it  may  be  well 
to  point  out  what  appear  to  be  characteristics  of  the  Sarum  Missal, 
and  tests  which  may  be  usefully  applied  to  separate  it  from  other 
Uses.  The  rite  belongs  to  the  great  family  of  Uses  which  have 
their  sources  in  the  liturgy  of  the  Roman  Church  and  which 
spread  gradually  over  the  continent  of  Western  Europe,  from 
Braga  and  Toledo  in  the  West  to  Drontheim  and  Upsala  in  the 
North.  It  is  not  in  the  Ordinary  or  Canon  of  the  Mass  that  the 
Sarum  characteristics  are  to  be  found.  What  was  once  thought 
to  be  particular  to  Sarum  or  derived  from  the  Ancient  Gallican 

^  See,  for  example,  the  long  gospel  of  the  passion  for  Palm  Sunday,  on  p.  98. 
"^  See  p.  123.  '  See  p.  413.  *  See  p.  419.  ^  p.  446. 

•  See  p.  131.  '  See  p.  102.  ^  p.  231. 


xiv  PREFACE 

Liturgy  may  be  found  in  other  Uses  or  even  in  the  Roman.^ 
But  by  comparison  of  the  variables  of  the  Sarum  Missal  with 
those  of  other  Uses  certain  differences  may  be  found  in  the 
Sarum,  especially  amongst  the  liturgical  sections  which  are  con- 
sidered by  many  to  be  as  old  as  any  portion  of  the  Mass,  the  Secrets 
and  the  Postcommons.  The  Collects  proper  are  in  most  cases  the 
same  as  those  in  the  Missal  of  Pope  Pius  V.  The  majority  of 
the  Secrets  and  Postcommons  are  also  the  same  as  the  Pian.  But 
here  and  there  in  the  Sarum  Missal  appear  Secrets  and  Post- 
commons  which  are  not  to  be  found  in  the  other  Uses,  though  they 
may  by  the  help  of  Mr.  H.  A.  Wilson's  invaluable  Index  to  the 
Roman  Sacramentaries  be  found  in  some  of  these.  One  of  the 
most  constant  peculiarities  of  the  Sarum  Use  that  I  have  yet  found 
is  the  Secret  for  the  second  Sunday  after  the  Epiphany  {Dominica 
secunda  post  octavas  Epiphaniae)  which  begins  Ut  tibi  grata.^ 
When  this  Secret  can  be  found  in  a  missal  the  opinion  may  be 
hazarded  that  the  book  is  of  Sarum  use.  It  may  be  found,  how- 
ever, in  the  Sacramentary  edited  by  Menard  ^  as  the  Secret  for  this 
Sunday,  and  also  in  the  Leonine  Sacramentary^  in  July,  with  the 
addition  of  a  second  clause  or  petition ;  but  not  in  any  of  the 
Missals  that  some  twenty  years  ago  ^  I  examined  for  the  edition  of 
the  Westminster  Missal. 

There  are  a  few  more  instances  in  which  the  Sarum  Postcommon 
has  not  yet  been  found  in  a  Use.  For  instance :  Dominica  v. 
post  Epiphaniam  has  a  Postcommon,  Dens  qui  nos  sacramenti^ 
which  has  not  been  found  in  other  Missals,  though  it  is  in  the 
Leonine  Sacramentary,'^  in  a  mass  for  December. 

So  also  in  Feria  iv.  post  Dominicam  ii.  Quadragesimae ;  as  Post- 
common  this  Wednesday  has  Prosit  nobis  Domine  quaesumns  ^ ;  but 
this  Postcommon  is  not  to  be  found  elsewhere,  as  far  as  I  have  looked. 

^  Some  years  ago  it  was  thought  in  certain  quarters  that  the  Sarum  Ordo  Missae  had 
its  roots  in  the  Gallican  or  Spanish  Liturgies,  the  so-called  Ephesine  Rite.  No  evidence 
for  this  theory  has  been  brought  forward  ;  and  as  at  the  present  moment  none  seems 
forthcoming,  it  is  hardly  worth  while  to  discuss  the  matter  here  at  length.

PREFACE  XV 

Again :  Dominica  Hi.  post  pascha  has  a  Postcommon,  Respice 
quaesuimis  Domine  popidum  tuum?-  The  British  Museum  Add. 
MS.  11414  has  this  Postcommon  also  on  this  Sunday,  and  the 
Gregorian  Sacramentary  on  the  Friday  in  Easter  week.^  It  is  also 
for  the  same  day  in  Menard,^  and  in  the  Sacramentary  edited  by 
Richter  and  Schoenfelder.^     But  I  have  yet  to  find  it  elsewhere. 

So  much  for  the  few  liturgical  sections  which  may  not  easily  be 
found  in  other  books.  It  may  very  well  be  supposed  that  before 
long  these  hitherto  unnoticed  collects  will  be  found  in  other  Uses. 

While  editing  the  Westminster  Missal,  there  came  across  my 
notice  a  small  group  of  English  monastic  missals  which  agreed  in 
certain  Secrets  and  Postcommons  with  those  in  the  Sarum  missal, 
but  not  with  the  Secrets  and  Postcommons  for  the  same  days  in  the 
Gregorian  Sacramentary  and  the  missals  which  follow  the  Gregorian 
Sacramentary.  The  group  includes  the  Missals  of  St.  Albans, 
Westminster,  Abingdon,  and  Tewkesbury.  The  variations  of  this 
'  Sarum '  group  from  the  Gregorian  are  many.  From  the  first 
Sunday  in  Advent  to  Easter  there  are  more  than  fifty  of  these 
varying  Secrets  and  Postcommons :  from  Easter  to  Advent  more 
than  twenty.  For  an  example  of  this :  on  the  Ember  Friday  in 
Advent  the  secret  is  a  collect  beginning  Sacrificiis  quaesiimus^ 
in  Sarum,  St.  Albans,  Westminster,  and  Tewkesbury,  while  the 
Gregorian  Sacramentary  has  Mimeribus  ttostris,  which  is  also  the 
reading  in  A,  a  true  Sarum  Missal. 

What  is  very  interesting,  many  of  these  variants  from  the 
Gregorian  are  not  to  be  found  in  any  part  of  the  three  Sacra- 
mentaries,  even  with  the  aid  of  Mr.  Wilson's  Index.  Nor  do  the 
variants  appear  in  the  earlier  Anglo-Saxon  books,  written  or  used 
in  England  before  or  shortly  after  the  Norman  Conquest,  such  as 
the  Leofric  and  Winchcombe  Missals,  the  Missal  of  Robert  of 
Jumieges,  or  the  Cotton  MS.  Vitellius  A.  xviii.  These  follow  closely 
the  Gregorian  collects  ;  so  that  one  is  led  to  the  suggestion  that 
these   Sarum   variants   may  have   been  introduced   into   English

churches  about  or  soon  after  the  time  of  the  Norman  Conquest.^ 
Some  do  certainly  appear  in  the  earlier  St.  Albans  Mass-book 
in  the  Bodleian  Library,  written  about  iioo. 

In  regard  to  later  variations  of  detail  it  may  be  worth  while  to 
note  that  the  Ordinary  of  the  Sarum  Mass  in  the  three  manuscripts  ^ 
is  not  the  same  as  that  in  the  printed  missals.  The  rubrics  are 
not  nearly  so  abundant  as  in  the  editions.  Evidence  is  given  of 
the  remains  of  the  practice  of  breaking  the  obley  at  the  word 
/regit  in  the  Canon.^  The  practice  of  elevating  the  host,  ut  videatur 
ab  omnibus,  is  well  developed  ;  but  not  so  that  of  the  chalice, 
which  is  only  raised  contra  pectus  at  consecration,  while  the  printed 
editions  direct  it  to  be  raised  usque  ad  pectus  vel  ultra  caput. 

In  C  and  A  Veni  Creator  is  said  at  the  beginning  of  Mass,  while 
in  the  printed  editions  this  hymn  is  to  be  said  while  vesting. 
B  and  M  have  special  prayers  for  each  vestment  *  and  Veni  Creator 
is  said  at  the  Offertory.  In  C  prayers  for  each  vestment^  have 
been  added  in  a  very  late  hand  in  a  vacant  space  at  the  bottom  of 
a  page. 

Further  notes  on  the  variants  of  the  Ordinary  in  C  may  be  found 
in  Tracts  on  the  Mass  issued  by  Plenry  Bradshaw  Society  in  1904.

I  can  hardly  sufficiently  express  my  sense  of  the  obligation  that 
I  am  under  to  Mr.  T.  Gambler- Parry  for  the  laborious  assistance 
that  he  gave  me  during  so  many  months,  I  think  I  must  say,  during

work,  and  in  the  severe  work  of  collating  the  text  of  Lord  Crawford's 
manuscript  with  those  from  the  Arsenal  at  Paris  and  from  the 
University  at  Bologna.

Note  as  to  a  Table  of  Contents 

In  place  of  the  usual  table  of  contents  arranged  according  to  the 
order  in  which  they  are  found  in  the  book,  it  has  been  thought 
that  perhaps  the  convenience  of  the  student  would  be  better  con- 
sulted if  an  index  of  the  contents  on  alphabetical  lines  were  added 
at  the  end  of  this  book  under  the  title  of  Index  of  Masses  and  other 
services.  Accordingly  this  index  of  contents  will  be  found  imme- 
diately before  the  index  of  liturgical  forms.

A  =  Paris,  Arsenal,  MS.  135.     Sarum  Missal. 

B  =  Bologna,  University,  MS.  2565.     Sarum  Missal.

cessional. 

When  words  are  followed  immediately  by  an  obelus  (t)  it  is  intended  thereby 
to  point  out  that  they  are  printed  as  in  the  manuscript  then  being  quoted. 


In  printing  the  Calendar  which  follows  immediately  an  attempt 
has  been  made  to  indicate  the  colours  used  by  the  scribe.  Thus 
small  capitals  represent  the  words  written  in  blue ;  italics  those 
written  in  red ;  and  Roman  those  written  in  black.  But  the  colour 
it  must  be  noted  is  no  certain  guide  to  the  grading  of  the  festival : 
otherwise  the  octave  of  the  Epiphany  would  be  of  higher  grading 
than  the  Epiphany  itself. 

The  crosses  enclosed  in  rectangular  figures  seem  to  indicate  the 
highest  festivals. 

The  symbol  f  appears  to  be  a  contraction  for  te  deum.
